The Real Cause of Deadly Medical Errors

Most cases that contribute to those eye-opening numbers are cases of hospital-acquired infections (come in for knee replacement, leave with pneumonia) or medication errors (get a drug that interacts adversely with another drug).

This happened to a former co-worker. He went to the hospital to get treatment for rheumatism and came out with a lung infection. One of the side effects of the drugs he was taking for the rheumatism was an increased susceptibility to infections, especially lung infections. The lung infection did him in over a number of years. His body slowly deteriorated until he could no longer work. He would get winded walking up one flight of stairs. The infection devastated his quality of life. From a practical standpoint though, the hospital he went to originally can't guarantee that you won't catch an infection. All they can realistically do is perform routine sanitation and let patients know ahead of time what certain risks of certain medications.

Doing what this author is suggesting would save lives, but I don't think it would appreciably lower the cases of hospital-acquired infections.

I can remember reading an article quite a few years ago that maintained that the rate of nosocomial (hospital acquired) infections was something like 60%. Understand I am operating from memory here. It could have been as low as 40%. The mercy was that the majority were airborne 'coughy/sneezies' that went away own their on with little trouble. Some, however, were serious like your friend's was. The rate, of course, would vary dramatically from hospital to hospital and from country to country. If I were to hazard a guess I'd guess that the 'best', in terms of safety, would be Germany and Switzerland and the worst amongst developed countries would be the USA - it would hardly be the only metric where America lands at the bottom of the heap in medical outcomes in developed countries.

There are a number of different reasons for the poor US performance, but I can see one here where the author's point might be relevant - the litigious nature of the USA. Removing the danger of lawsuits could do wonders for encouraging honesty, and honesty improves outcomes.

It's not surprising to see the USA at the bottom of the heap on some of these statistics. I heard a few years ago that Canada had a unique system for handling lawsuits. Essentially that most doctors were pooled together and most lawsuits were strenuously fought, thereby eliminating a lot of frivolous lawsuits, thus lowering costs. Okay, here is a wikipedia link: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Medical_Protective_Association

I really wish we could cherry pick best practices from other countries. You are 100% right about honesty. It sounds quaint, but honesty and trust mean so much in everything from personal relationships to business transactions. I think it would be better to reduce the danger of lawsuits rather than remove them altogether, but it seems that the threat of lawsuits changes peoples behavior, and not for the greater good.
